task_retrieval_key:
A 3-year-old boy, the only child of non-consanguineous parents, exhibited widespread warty eruptions covering the body, including the genital area, but excluding the scalp, face, palms, and soles. The skin changes began at 3 weeks of age, initially appearing symmetrically on the anterior thighs, then spreading to the axillae, and over approximately 6 months, progressed to the current widespread distribution. There was no history of blisters or generalized redness at or after birth. The condition showed improvement during summer and worsened in winter. The child was otherwise in good health with no developmental delays or visual or hearing difficulties. There was no significant family history. Physical examination revealed multiple, bilaterally symmetrical, verrucous plaques following the lines of Blaschko, extensively involving the trunk and extremities. The plaques were oriented transversely on the trunk and longitudinally on the limbs. Hair, nails, and oral cavity appeared normal. Systemic examination showed no abnormalities.
